title: Whose work was it?
text: A classmate wants the display to list only their name, though you did half the work.

outcomes.text: We listed what each of us had done. It was fair, if a little awkward.
We made room for both names, then argued about whose section looked better.

choices.label: Ask the teacher to set clear roles

outcomes.text: The teacher helped us divide the work. The presentation improved; my classmate stayed annoyed.
The teacher asked us to solve it together. We did, slowly.
I let the display go forward. The grade was fine; the credit still bothered me.
My classmate thanked me, then never mentioned the work again.

title: Can you cover?
text: A coworker needs a shift covered at short notice. Your own week is already full.

outcomes.text: We agreed on a shift swap. It cost a free evening, but the arrangement was fair.
I covered the shift. We never settled the promised swap, and I was tired for days.
I explained what I could manage. My coworker was disappointed, but understood.
They took the refusal personally. We were civil at work and distant outside it.

choices.label: Ask the manager to arrange coverage

outcomes.text: The manager found cover and changed the rota. Neither of us had to rescue the schedule alone.
The manager found cover, though my coworker wished I had handled it privately.

title: The club costs more this year
text: Your child wants to stay in an activity, but the new fees strain the household budget.

outcomes.text: We worked through the numbers and found a smaller plan the household could manage.
The numbers were worse than I expected. We agreed to revisit it after payday.
My child stayed in the club. I had to trim another part of the household budget.
The fee was still a stretch. I paid it and worried about the next bill.
We found a community group with a smaller fee. It was different, but still theirs.
The alternative did not fit. My child felt I had decided before listening.

title: A friend checks in
text: A close friend writes that keeping in touch has felt one-sided lately.

choices.label: Make a realistic plan to call

outcomes.text: We picked a time that worked for both of us. It was small, and we kept it.
We made a plan, then both weeks filled up. At least we were honest about it.
I listened without defending myself. We talked about what each of us could manage.
The apology helped, but the distance had already changed the friendship.
We wished each other well. The friendship mattered, even as it became quieter.
My silence answered for me. I missed them more than I expected.

title: The second diagnosis
text: A repair is nearly finished when {them.first} spots a sound neither of you can place.

outcomes.text: We traced the sound to a loose bracket and recorded the repair before handing the vehicle back.
The check found nothing urgent. We documented the uncertainty and booked another inspection.

choices.label: Ask a senior technician to review it

outcomes.text: The senior technician found a missed step. We corrected it and added it to the checklist.
The review backed our first diagnosis. The extra check took time, but gave us a clear record.

choices.label: Close the ticket and move on

outcomes.text: The repair passed a short check, though {them.first} was uneasy about the thin notes.

title: A careful handover
text: At shift change, {them.first} is interrupted before they can finish passing on the day’s notes.

outcomes.text: We took a few more minutes to check the notes and make sure the next shift knew what remained open.
We completed the notes, though the late finish made the trip home harder.

choices.label: Ask the supervisor to rebalance the shift

outcomes.text: The supervisor assigned a second person to the remaining work. The handover was complete without one person carrying it all.
There was no extra cover. We agreed what could safely wait and recorded it clearly.
I left on time. The unfinished handover came back as a difficult conversation at the next shift.

title: A lesson that missed
text: A class struggled with a lesson you prepared. {them.first} offers to compare notes before the next one.

choices.label: Compare the lesson and revise one section

outcomes.text: We found where the instructions lost the class and built in a short practice example.
The revised plan helped some students, though the whole unit still needs work.

choices.label: Ask the class what was unclear

outcomes.text: Their feedback was specific. I changed the examples and explained why.
The feedback was mixed. I kept what worked and scheduled another review.

choices.label: Blame the class for not trying

outcomes.text: The complaint was easy. The next lesson went just as poorly, and {them.first} stopped offering help.

title: One more review
text: A deadline is close when {them.first} asks you to look at a change that affects several other parts of the project.

outcomes.text: We caught a mismatch before it reached the rest of the team and wrote down what still needed review.
The change passed review, but only after we trimmed its scope to fit the deadline.

choices.label: Record the risk and ask for more time

outcomes.text: The deadline moved. It was awkward to explain, but the team approved the extra review time.
The date stayed fixed, so we agreed which parts would wait for the next release.
The delivery was quick. A review request came back the next morning, and {them.first} had to explain the missed check too.

title: Borrowed without asking
text: {them.first} borrowed pieces from your project and forgot to put them back.

outcomes.text: We sorted the pieces and rebuilt a smaller version. My sibling learned why asking matters.
We found most of the pieces. The missing part stayed annoying, but we stopped blaming each other.

choices.label: Ask a parent to help us agree

outcomes.text: We agreed which things we could share and which needed permission. The rule worked both ways.
The rule was clear. My sibling felt embarrassed about needing an adult to settle it.
I hid their things. Now we both guarded our rooms instead of playing together.
They found the hiding place and returned my pieces, but the argument lasted longer than the project.

title: Home later than planned
text: You stayed out later than agreed. {them.first} was waiting up, worried.

outcomes.text: We agreed on one message when plans change. More freedom came with a clear responsibility.
We agreed on messages, though the old curfew stayed for now. Trust needed more than tonight.

choices.label: Ask what they were afraid of

outcomes.text: Their worry made more sense once I listened. We planned a safer way home together.
The conversation was tense. We took a break and agreed to discuss it when rested.

choices.label: Say it is none of their business

outcomes.text: The argument ended with tighter rules and less trust on both sides.
They stopped asking for details. The silence felt less like freedom than I expected.

title: Always available?
text: {them.first} sends messages late every night. You care, but you need sleep too.

choices.label: Set a time we can both manage

outcomes.text: We chose a regular check-in. I slept better, and they knew when I would listen.
They felt rejected at first. A shorter daytime call helped explain that the friendship still mattered.
They needed more support than one friend could give. We talked about other people they could reach.
They were not ready to explain. I offered company without promising to answer all night.
They felt heard, but I arrived exhausted the next morning. Caring needed a more sustainable plan.
Sleep loss made me snap at a harmless message. We both wished I had set a limit sooner.

title: A quieter weekday
text: {them.first} suggests a regular weekday visit. Your routines have changed with age.

outcomes.text: A small recurring visit gave both weeks a familiar shape. Neither of us had to host a whole occasion.
Travel tired us more than expected. We kept the friendship and shortened the visit.

choices.label: Invite them for a simple lunch

outcomes.text: We used what was already in the kitchen and caught up without making it a production.
Our schedules missed each other. A phone call still made the afternoon feel less empty.
I explained that I needed quiet. We agreed that declining one visit was not ending the friendship.
I left the invitation unanswered. They stopped suggesting dates, and I missed the company.

title: Do we both want this?
text: {them.first} wants a household purchase you do not think you need. It is time to discuss the budget.

outcomes.text: We chose a limit and checked what each of us valued. The conversation mattered more than the item.
We agreed on the limit but not the purchase. We paused it instead of quietly buying it anyway.

choices.label: Try what we already own first

outcomes.text: We rearranged what we had. It worked well enough to save the purchase for another year.
The old item really was worn out. I admitted it and we planned rather than argued.
The item was never the whole point. My partner felt excluded from a decision about our shared home.
We dropped the purchase, but the next budget conversation carried the same resentment.

title: The changed order
text: During a busy service, {them.first} notices that an allergy note was lost from an order.

outcomes.text: We checked the note, remade the dish and told the serving team. The delay protected the guest.
The safe replacement took longer than promised. We explained the delay and kept the kitchen informed.

choices.label: Ask the shift lead to coordinate

outcomes.text: The shift lead separated the preparation and corrected the ticket process. Everyone knew the next step.
The lead was busy too. We held the order until someone could check it properly.

choices.label: Send it and hope it is fine

outcomes.text: My coworker stopped the dish before it left. I had to explain why I ignored the warning.
The serving team caught the missing note. Service stopped while the kitchen reviewed what went wrong.
